claims.text: Machine-learning optimization of SPS temperature, pressure, and time will produce a uniformly dense W–Cu composite with minimal voids.
The proposed process will overcome phase separation associated with conventional W–Cu powder processing.
The initial material consists of tungsten particles or interconnected tungsten regions within a copper matrix.
Baseline W–Cu processing exhibits voids and inhomogeneous copper penetration.
A machine-learning framework can systematically determine and control suitable SPS temperature, pressure, and duration.
SPS can employ high pressure and short sintering times.
The relevant SPS temperature should approach tungsten's melting regime while remaining below tungsten melting and avoiding copper boiling.
The resulting microstructure will have uniform copper infiltration through the tungsten skeleton, near-perfect interfacial contact, and minimized voids.
The machine-learning model will use real-time data and historical processing outcomes to identify narrow SPS processing windows.
Rapid processing kinetics cause void formation and phase separation in W–Cu.
Control within the identified processing window will improve phase mixing and mechanical interlocking.
Improved phase mixing and mechanical interlocking will enhance thermal conductivity and mechanical durability.
ML-optimized SPS will yield lower porosity and greater uniformity than conventional SPS or powder metallurgy.
The optimized W–Cu composite will have improved thermal transport and greater mechanical resilience under fusion-relevant irradiation and temperature conditions.
Conventional SPS and infiltration leave residual voids and uneven copper penetration that impair thermal transport.
SPS can produce fine or controlled microstructures with high density or low porosity.
The proposal is limited to small-to-moderate-scale fusion-reactor joint components and requires further validation for scale-up and prolonged irradiation.
The ability of machine-learning optimization to eliminate defects robustly across batch sizes and long-term service conditions remains empirically uncertain.
